paragraphs: One-sentence judgment: a bicycle repairer is not “someone who can change an inner tube,” but a technical position that inspects, repairs, adjusts, assembles, and maintains bicycles according to manufacturer specifications and work sequence: receiving the bicycle and asking about riding use and symptoms, performing visual and functional inspection and locating faults by symptom, estimating labor and parts and opening a repair work order, installing and adjusting shifting and gearing, installing and adjusting brakes and brake pads, installing new tires and inner tubes, cleaning and lubricating parts, truing wheels (lateral and radial), disassembling and assembling axles to repair or adjust or replace defective parts, installing and replacing accessories and attachments such as handlebars and lights and saddles, adjusting riding position to the customer's build and use, and explaining repair plans and parts trade-offs to customers; it is not suitable for people who tighten screws by feel only, are unwilling to verify torque and clearance against model manuals and specifications, and are unwilling to treat brake and wheel rechecks and work order records as part of the job.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to repeatedly locate the same mechanical error until the recheck passes, you can keep details consistent using hands and visual inspection and measuring tools, you recheck brakes and wheels and fasteners in order and stop when out of specification, you are willing to check the manual before starting when the model or part version is unclear, you can explain technical trade-offs in language the customer understands, and you can truthfully record work orders and parts and torque and exceptions.

Conditions for pausing investment first: you have not yet completed a full receive—inspect—locate—adjust—recheck—hand over loop under any supervised conditions, or you can only explain your interest by saying “I have repaired my own bike”; also do not treat personal disassembly experience or a hobby course as proof that you can independently judge whether brakes and wheels and fasteners are safe, or independently release a bicycle for the road. Specifications for brakes and fasteners and wheel tension, the compatibility of e-assist and batteries and chargers, the use of greases and cleaners and tools, customer information and vehicle information handling, and inspection and release and stoppage authority must be carried out in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and the employer and the manufacturer manual and must leave traceable records; this page does not provide any torque values, assembly sequence, or methods for modification and removing speed limits.

Occupational identity and definition must be verified separately: O*NET lists 49-3091.00 (Bicycle Repairers) as Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0), and the page lists only three education levels (some jobs require a high school diploma or equivalent, some require having attended college without a degree, and some require less than a high school diploma) without publishing the percentage at each level; the page also does not mark this occupation as Bright Outlook, and the employment projection is a decline (the employment trends page gives 13,200 in 2024 falling to about 12,900 in 2034, -2%, while still projecting about 1,600 annual openings over the projection period). It must also be noted: the wage, employment, and industry data on this page are all under this occupation's separate definition on the O*NET page (the page does not contain labels such as “Wage data for …” or “Employment data for …” taken from another occupation). Education, occupational training, industry certification, employer hiring and store task authorization, and jurisdictional requirements involving e-assist and batteries and modification and removing speed limits are different statuses and must be verified item by item according to employer and position and jurisdiction.

In one sentence: this is a technical position that delivers steadily by verifying item by item against model manuals and specifications and working through the rhythm of repeatedly locating mechanical errors and rechecking, with the core being repair and adjustment and brake and wheel rechecks and work order records — not an interest in cycling or an imagination about social media; its U.S. wage and employment are under this occupation's separate definition, and growth is projected to be negative.

The work of bicycle repairers can be divided into three categories: repair and adjustment services (receiving bicycles and asking about riding use and symptoms; performing visual and functional inspection and locating faults by symptom; estimating labor and parts and opening repair work orders; installing and adjusting shifting and gearing; installing and adjusting brakes and brake pads; installing new tires and inner tubes; cleaning and lubricating parts; truing wheels and checking spoke tension; disassembling and assembling axles to repair or adjust or replace defective parts; installing and replacing accessories and attachments such as handlebars and kickstands and lights and saddles; adjusting riding position to the customer's build and use; cutting new spokes for wheel building as needed; dressing replacement parts with a bench grinder; patching inner tubes as needed); assembly and sales and store operations (assembling new bicycles; selling bicycles and accessories; helping customers choose bicycles by build and use; ordering parts and accessories; cleaning and organizing the workstation and tools; maintaining repair and parts and torque and recheck records); and customer reception and explanation (explaining technical trade-offs and costs and waiting times to customers; handling pickup and rework and complaints; explaining boundaries according to procedure on matters involving e-assist and batteries and brakes and modification). All three categories presume stopping to verify first when the model or part version does not match, the brake or wheel or frame recheck does not pass, the e-assist or battery condition is unknown, or the situation exceeds your authorization.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET 49-3091.00 Bicycle Repairers (page updated 2026, not marked Bright Outlook). The official duties are to repair and maintain bicycles; there are 20 official tasks (15 core, 3 supplemental, and 2 New added tasks, all counted within the total of 20, with New having no score), with core task importance scores from 93 to 60 and supplemental tasks of 65 and 41 and 26. The work activities page lists 41 items with importance scores, the highest being making decisions and solving problems 87, identifying objects, actions, and events 86, getting information 83, handling and moving objects 82, inspecting equipment, structures, or materials 82, influencing others or selling 80, communicating with people outside the organization 78, updating and using relevant knowledge 77, resolving conflicts and negotiating with others 76, estimating the quantifiable characteristics of products, events, or information 75, performing for or working directly with the public 75, and repairing and maintaining mechanical equipment 73. There are 21 detailed work activities (no scores). The task list describes group work and does not mean every position performs all tasks.

entries: Receiving and asking | Give the repair a basis | Receive the bicycle and ask clearly about riding use and symptoms, record the model and part version and the customer's description, and explain the repairable scope and waiting time.
Inspection and location | Make the fault reproducible | Perform visual and functional inspection, locate the fault by symptom, and distinguish adjustable problems from already damaged parts.

Repair and adjustment | Give the result a specification | Disassemble and assemble and adjust and clean and lubricate according to the manufacturer manual and specifications, and install and adjust brakes and shifting and replace tires and inner tubes.

Recheck and test ride | Make release reviewable | Recheck brakes and wheels and fasteners according to specifications and test ride to confirm when necessary; bicycles that do not meet specifications are not released.
Work orders and parts | Make the process traceable | Open repair work orders and record parts and labor and costs and specifications, and order and verify parts and batches.

Handover and explanation | Let the customer judge | Explain the repair plan and parts trade-offs and follow-up notes to the customer, handle rework and complaints within the authorized scope, and record exceptions.

Work environment | 98% have face-to-face discussions every day, 92% have telephone conversations every day, 41% are in contact with others continuously (another 59% most of the time), 36% work at moderate proximity (arm's length) to others, and 11% consider dealing with external customers or the public very important; 78% continuously or almost continuously stand (another 17% more than half the time), 91% sit less than half the time, 24% continuously or almost continuously need to keep their balance (another 56% less than half the time and 17% never), 11% bend or twist the body about half the time, and 89% never climb ladders or scaffolds; indoors without environmental control: 76% at least once a week and 12% never; the page this round does not show a daily proportion, 26% are outdoors in all weather every day, 24% are exposed to contaminants every day, 11% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise at least once a week, 14% encounter minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings at least once a year, and 12% never come into contact with hazardous equipment; 91% consider the work not at all automated and 98% consider the pace determined by equipment speed not at all important; the page also has about 29 context items (including whether common or specialized protective equipment is worn, time pressure, and frequency and precision requirements) whose percentage distributions are not published, and this page does not fill in values on their behalf.
Main equipment and tools | Hand tools (hex keys, sockets, wrenches, spoke wrenches, chain tools), specialized measuring tools (spoke tension meters, calipers, specification gauges) and truing equipment, lifts and repair stands and workbenches, cleaners and lubricants and solvents and greases, bench grinders and welding and painting equipment (according to position scope), tire and inner tube and tubeless system tools, repair management software and point-of-sale systems, and personal protection (eye protection and gloves and ventilation as the work requires).
Task rhythm | 11% have a typical workweek of less than 40 hours (the rest of the distribution is not published); 65% have a lot of freedom in decisions and 32% some freedom; 62% have a lot of freedom in determining tasks and priorities and 28% some freedom; 80% consider competition moderate; 23% consider repeating the same tasks very important; 13% are in conflict situations at least once a month; 24% consider the consequences of error extremely serious.
Collaboration | Collaborate with technicians and sales and inventory staff in the same shop; 12% consider working with a work group or team very important; 32% bear very high responsibility for others' work results and outcomes; 11% bear moderate responsibility for the health and safety of others.
Compliance and safety | Repair and adjustment and assembly must be carried out according to the manufacturer manual and specifications for the specific model and parts; where e-assist and lithium-ion batteries and chargers are involved, use chargers provided or recommended by the manufacturer and batteries confirmed as compatible, and do not use battery packs that have been modified or reworked by unqualified persons; this guidance does not provide repair authorization and recommends charging while someone is present (U.S. CPSC micromobility product safety guidance); on the mainland China side, electric bicycles are subject to the mandatory national standard GB 17761-2024 Safety Technical Specification for Electric Bicycles (issued 2024-12-31, effective 2025-09-01, fully replacing GB 17761-2018), with CCC product certification for related production / certification / sales, not a repair technician license; O*NET lists 1 national certification (Certified Bicycle Technician).
Records and retrospective | Work orders and model and part version, faults and the locating process, adjustments performed and specifications, brake and wheel and fastener recheck results, parts and labor and costs, and customer feedback and exceptions need to be traceable.
Skills and training | O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0); basic skills are led by active listening 66, critical thinking 63, reading comprehension 50, speaking 50, monitoring 44, and writing 44; transferable skills are led by repairing 72, troubleshooting 60, service orientation 56, time management 53, equipment maintenance 50, quality control analysis 50, social perceptiveness 50, complex problem solving 47, equipment selection 47, and installation 47; knowledge is led by mechanical 92, customer and personal service 86, sales and marketing 69, public safety and security 65, production and processing 60, and engineering and technology 58 (33 items in total with scores); there are 52 abilities in total with scores (near vision 72, finger dexterity 69, visualization 69, arm-hand steadiness 66, and others); there are 19 work styles, with attention to detail 75, dependability 71, and caution 50; these are occupational characteristic scores, not individual thresholds.
Entry and authorization | Education and certification do not equal inspection and release or modification determination authority; the O*NET educational composition lists only three levels and does not publish proportions, and jobs in this zone require experience ranging from little to a few months and on-the-job training ranging from a few days to a year; O*NET lists 1 national certification, which does not equal a hiring threshold or employer appointment.
Industry and employers | The O*NET industry distribution is retail trade 80% and other industries (including real estate and rental and leasing and other services) 20%; the editor lists as job-search verification scenarios: brand stores, independent bike shops, sporting goods retail repair, and shared mobility operations; no occupational share sample for each type of employer was obtained this round.

All six directions share a background of mechanical inspection and disassembly and measurement and safety basics, but their work objects, deliverables, and specification and authorization requirements differ; the same repair or adjustment experience cannot be directly converted into another direction's qualification or task and release authorization (for example, automobiles and motorcycles involve stricter road and emissions compliance), and this page only compares differences in duties under public definitions.

The basis for comparison is the official occupational description of O*NET 49-3091.00 and the related occupations list on the O*NET page, as well as the adjacent occupation relationships indicated in the routing materials; an adjacent relationship only describes proximity of duties and does not mean that qualifications, authorizations, or positions are interchangeable.

The table below compares bicycle repairers with five adjacent directions along the same set of dimensions: occupational direction, core work and output, key differences, and which option better suits each preference.

Automotive service technicians and mechanics handle whole-vehicle power and electronic systems and diagnostics and are usually subject to stricter emissions and safety and lifting standards; bicycle repairers work on human-powered bicycles and their mechanical and some e-assist peripheral systems.

If you prefer whole-vehicle power and electronic diagnostics, compare automotive service technicians and mechanics first; if you prefer repairing and adjusting human-powered bicycles and light systems, bicycle repairers are suitable.
Complete whole-vehicle repair and diagnostics and maintenance according to model specifications, with output mainly repair work orders and diagnostic records.
Bicycle repairers and automotive service technicians and mechanics

Motorcycle mechanics handle engines and motor vehicle systems and fuel and drivetrain and usually involve more complex powertrains and stricter road compliance; bicycle repairers mainly work on human-powered drivetrains and brakes and wheels.
If you prefer engines and motor vehicle systems, compare motorcycle mechanics first; if you prefer light human-powered systems, bicycle repairers are suitable.
Complete engine and drivetrain and brake repair according to model specifications, with output mainly work orders and compliance records.
Bicycle repairers and motorcycle mechanics

Electric motor and power tool repairers handle motors and portable power tools and power systems, focusing on electrical and insulation and motor windings; bicycle repairers focus on mechanical adjustment, with e-assist involved only in peripheral installation and compatibility verification.
If you prefer motors and electrical systems, compare electric motor and power tool repairers first; if you prefer mechanical adjustment and assembly, bicycle repairers are suitable.
Complete testing and repair of motors and power tools, with output mainly electrical test and repair records.
Bicycle repairers and electric motor and power tool repairers

Outdoor power equipment and other small engine mechanics handle garden and power equipment and small engines and usually involve fuel and ignition and emissions systems; bicycle repairers mainly work on human-powered drive systems and wheels and brakes.
If you prefer small engines and garden equipment, compare that direction first; if you prefer human-powered drive and bicycle systems, bicycle repairers are suitable.
Complete repair and maintenance of small engines and garden equipment, with output mainly work orders and maintenance records.
Bicycle repairers and outdoor power equipment and other small engine mechanics

Tire repairers and changers focus on mounting and repairing and replacing tires and rims and usually do not handle whole-wheel brake and shifting adjustment; bicycle repairers also handle wheel truing and brake and shifting adjustment.
If you prefer specializing in tire and rim work, compare tire repairers and changers first; if you prefer whole-bicycle mechanical adjustment, bicycle repairers are suitable.
Complete mounting and repairing and balancing of tires and rims, with output mainly tire work orders.
Bicycle repairers and tire repairers and changers

Recreational vehicle service technicians handle the broader body and facility and plumbing and electrical systems of motorhomes and recreational vehicles, with different work objects and standards systems; bicycle repairers work on the lightweight vehicle mechanical systems used mainly for riding.
If you prefer body and facility systems, compare recreational vehicle service technicians first; if you prefer lightweight vehicle mechanical systems, bicycle repairers are suitable.
Complete repair and maintenance of recreational vehicle body and facility systems, with output mainly work orders and inspection records.
Bicycle repairers and recreational vehicle service technicians

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the work object and deliverable results and specification and authorization requirements, not whether both do mechanical repair; after choosing a direction, verify item by item the training, qualifications, and task and release authorization requirements of the target direction.

entries.answer: The key risks include incorrect braking mode or fasteners, rim or spoke damage, grease contaminating braking surfaces, mismatched e-assist batteries or chargers, and handing over a bicycle with unresolved faults; the control method is to adjust according to the manufacturer model manual, use appropriate tools and eye protection, recheck brakes and wheels and fasteners in order and refuse unsafe release; where lithium-ion batteries are involved, use only chargers provided or recommended by the manufacturer and batteries confirmed as compatible, do not handle battery packs that have been modified or reworked, and charge while someone is present; also attend to protection against prolonged standing and repeated bending and chemical and debris injuries.

hero.quick_answer: Bicycle repairers inspect, repair, adjust, assemble, and maintain bicycles: receiving bicycles and asking about riding use and symptoms, performing visual and functional inspection and locating faults by symptom, estimating labor and parts and opening repair work orders, installing and adjusting shifting and gearing, installing and adjusting brakes and brake pads, installing new tires and inner tubes, cleaning and lubricating parts, truing wheels (including lateral and radial), disassembling and assembling axles to repair or adjust or replace defective parts, installing and replacing accessories and attachments such as handlebars and kickstands and lights and saddles, adjusting riding position to the customer's build and use, cutting new spokes for wheel building as needed, dressing replacement parts with a bench grinder, and explaining repair plans and parts trade-offs to customers; their work does not equal judging on the customer's behalf whether a bicycle may continue on the road, nor does it replace the release determination for model manuals and brake and fastener and battery-related specifications, and they stop and escalate when the model does not match, a part is damaged, the brake or wheel recheck does not pass, or the situation exceeds their authorization.

subject.summary: Bicycle repairers inspect, repair, adjust, assemble, and maintain bicycles: receiving bicycles and asking about symptoms, visual and functional inspection, locating faults, estimating labor and parts and opening work orders, installing and adjusting shifting and braking, replacing tires and inner tubes, cleaning and lubricating parts, truing wheels, disassembling and assembling axles to replace defective parts, installing and replacing accessories and attachments, adjusting riding position to the customer's build and use, and explaining repair plans to customers.
